Peshmerga: Internal security forces of Iraq's Kurdistan Region. The Peshmerga (Kurdish: پێشمەرگه, romanized: Pêşmerge, lit. ''Those Who Face Death'') are the internal security forces of the Kurdistan Region.
This former army chief seized power in a 2014 coup, installed a military junta, and went on to serve as Thailand's prime minister for nearly a decade. Who is he?
Prayut Chan-o-cha: Prime Minister of Thailand from 2014 to 2023.
Considered the ideal man in Hindu tradition, this seventh avatar of the god Vishnu was born in Ayodhya to King Dasaratha and later married Sita — who is he?
Mixing anti-elitist rhetoric with neo-nationalism, social conservatism, and a vow to defend national culture from outsiders — which political ideology is this?

Right-wing populism: Political ideology. Right-wing populism, also called right populism and national populism, is a political ideology that combines right-wing politics with populist rhetoric and themes.
Often called the first European war of the 21st century, this August 2008 conflict erupted over the breakaway regions of South Ossetia and Abkhazia — which war?
Russo-Georgian War: 2008 war between Russia and Georgia.
Founded in Japan in 2020 by Sohei Kamiya, this far-right populist party surged to more than 14 seats and third place in the 2025 House of Councillors election — which party?
The longest-serving president in his country's republican history, this Italian statesman has held office since 2015 and helped found the Democratic Party in 2007 — who is he?
Sergio Mattarella: President of Italy since 2015. Sergio Mattarella (born 23 July 1941) is an Italian politician who has been serving as the president of Italy since 2015.

Forced into exile as a child when Bulgaria's monarchy was abolished in 1946, this former Tsar returned five decades later to become the country's prime minister after winning the 2001 election — who is he?
Simeon II: Tsar of Bulgaria from 1943 to 1946, Prime Minister from 2001 to 2005.

Born in Trinidad, this civil rights leader helped launch the Black Power movement while heading SNCC, then served as 'Honorary Prime Minister' of the Black Panther Party — and later took the name Kwame Ture. Who was he?
This Umayyad commander crossed from North Africa to launch the Muslim conquest of the Iberian Peninsula in 711, leaving his name forever attached to the rock where he massed his troops — who is he?
Tariq ibn Ziyad: Umayyad commander in Hispania (died c. 720)
Before becoming the Supreme Court's first African-American justice, he argued 32 civil rights cases before it and won 29 — culminating in the landmark Brown v. Board of Education. Who was he?
Thurgood Marshall: US Supreme Court justice from 1967 to 1991.

Born in Ohio and originally named Hiram, this West Point graduate led the Vicksburg campaign that seized control of the Mississippi River before becoming the Union's top general and eventually the 18th U.S. president — who is he?
Ulysses S. Grant: Civil War general, U.S. president from 1869 to 1877.
While imprisoned at Ratnagiri in 1923, this Indian politician coined the Hindu-nationalist ideology of Hindutva and had earlier co-founded a secret society called Abhinav Bharat — who was he?
Vinayak Damodar Savarkar: Indian politician and ideologue (1883–1966)

Named after the city where its constitution was drafted, this German state of 1918 to 1933 marked the country's first constitutional experiment of its kind — a label later coined by Hitler in 1929 — what was it called?
Weimar Republic: German state from 1918 to 1933. The state was officially named the German Reich; but was more commonly referred to, and unofficially proclaimed itself, as the German Republic.
An assistant marshal to his brother Virgil, this lawman is famously credited as the key figure in the 1881 gunfight at the O.K. Corral — who is he?

This Polish politician served two stints as justice minister — one ending under PM Mateusz Morawiecki in 2023 — while also holding the prosecutor general post and championing an anti-corruption crusade — who is he?
Who among these was born first?
Patrick Geddes (born 1854) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these people was born first?
Patrick Geddes (born 1854) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four began earliest?
COBOL (founded 1959) is the earliest of the four. COBOL (Common Business-Oriented Language;) is a compiled English-like computer programming language designed for business use.
Which of these four came first?
MATLAB (founded 1984) is the earliest of the four. MATLAB (Matrix Laboratory) is a proprietary multi-paradigm programming language and numeric computing environment developed by MathWorks.
Who among these is a physicist?
Which of these is a mathematician?
Emmy Noether is a mathematician. Amalie Emmy Noether (23 March 1882 – 14 April 1935) was a German mathematician who made many important contributions to abstract algebra.
What is the atomic number of Meitnerium?
Meitnerium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Mt and atomic number 109.
What is the atomic number of Rubidium?
Rubidium is a chemical element; it has symbol Rb and atomic number 37.
In what year was Pope Benedict XVI born?
Pope Benedict XVI: Following his resignation, he chose to be known as "pope emeritus", a title he held until his death on 31 December 2022.
In what year was Javier Milei born?
Javier Milei: Javier Gerardo Milei (born 22 October 1970) is an Argentine politician and economist who has served as the 57th president of Argentina since 2023.
In what year was Piero Ferrari born?
Piero Ferrari (born Piero Lardi, 22 May 1945; later Piero Lardi Ferrari) is an Italian billionaire businessman and sport personality.
In what year did Giordano Bruno die?
Giordano Bruno: Bruno's pantheism was not taken lightly by the church, nor was his teaching of metempsychosis regarding the reincarnation of the soul.
In what year did Erwin Schrödinger die?
Erwin Schrödinger: Schrödinger shared the 1933 Nobel Prize in Physics with Paul Dirac "for the discovery of new productive forms of atomic theory".
In what year was Silicon discovered?
Silicon (SILL-ih-kən) is a chemical element; it has symbol Si and atomic number 14.
Which company manufactures Antonov An-124 Ruslan?
Antonov An-124 Ruslan: Aviastar-SP. The An-124 remains the largest military transport aircraft in service.
In which country is Mil Mi-8?
Mil Mi-8: Burkina Faso. The Mi-8 is the world's most-produced helicopter, with over 17,000 units used by over 50 countries.
Who is credited with discovering Antlia?
Antlia: Nicolas Louis de Lacaille. Antlia (from Ancient Greek ἀντλία) is a constellation in the Southern Celestial Hemisphere.
Who is credited with discovering Factitious disorder imposed on another?
Factitious disorder imposed on another: Roy Meadow. The victim is typically the caregiver's child but is occasionally an adult partner.
Who is credited with discovering Trisomy 18?
Trisomy 18: John H. Edwards. Trisomy 18, also known as Edwards syndrome, is a genetic disorder.
Who is credited with discovering Strontium?
Strontium: William Cruickshank. Strontium is a chemical element; it has symbol Sr and atomic number 38.
A "classic organochlorine" insecticide once heavily used to treat seed and soil, it was banned in most countries by the 1990s after proving a persistent, bioaccumulating pollutant. What is it?
Aldrin is an organochlorine insecticide that was widely used until the 1990s, when it was banned in most countries.
This order of ray-finned fish is named for a modified fin ray that dangles like bait to lure in prey, much like a human with a fishing rod — what are they called?

Anglerfish are ray-finned fish in the order Lophiiformes. The majority are bottom-dwellers, being demersal fish, while the aberrant deep-sea anglerfish are pelagic, (mostly) living high in the water column.
Founder of a prominent Russian design studio and an avid, famously foul-mouthed blogger, this designer and entrepreneur is also a member of the Tolstoy family — name this designer?
Artemy Lebedev (born 13 February 1975) is a Russian designer, entrepreneur and Internet personality.
These nocturnal blood-feeding insects from the genus Cimex can trigger skin rashes, itching, and even psychological distress from their bites — what are they commonly called?
Bed bug are insects from the genus Cimex, which are parasites that feed on blood, usually at night.

Believed to descend from hounds kept at a Belgian abbey and used by police worldwide to track escaped prisoners, this scent hound can discern a person's trail days after they've passed — name this dog breed?
Bloodhound is a large scent hound, originally bred for hunting deer, wild boar, rabbits, and since the Middle Ages, for tracking people.

This opioid medication used to treat addiction and pain can be delivered under the tongue, through the cheek, by injection, patch, or implant — and is often combined with naloxone to deter misuse — what drug is it?
Buprenorphine is an opioid used to treat opioid use disorder, acute pain, and chronic pain.
Which Mediterranean evergreen tree, grown mainly in Spain, produces edible seed pods often ground into a chocolate substitute, with seeds that yield a gum used as a food thickener?
Carob (Ceratonia siliqua) is a flowering evergreen tree or shrub in the Caesalpinioideae subfamily of the legume family, Fabaceae.
The principal sterol of all animals, it concentrates in the brain and spinal cord and is essential to every cell membrane — yet too much in the blood spells trouble. What is it?
Cholesterol is the principal sterol of all animals, distributed in body tissues, especially the brain and spinal cord, and in animal fats and oils.

The most widely distributed corvid, this large all-black bird is found across the Northern Hemisphere and is the heaviest passerine bird, with 11 accepted subspecies showing little variation in appearance. What bird is this?
Common raven (Corvus corax) is a large all-black passerine bird.
The third most-produced American fighter of the Second World War, trailing only the Mustang and the Thunderbolt, this plane first took flight in 1938 — which aircraft?
Curtiss P-40 Warhawk is an American single-engined, single-seat, all-metal fighter-bomber that first flew in 1938.
First discovered in 1877 and named the following year for its unique double-beamed tail bones, this genus of long-necked sauropod dinosaur roamed Late Jurassic North America — what is it?
Diplodocus (or) is an extinct genus of diplodocid sauropod dinosaurs known from the Late Jurassic of North America.
These extinct flightless giants of Madagascar — possibly the largest birds ever, laying the biggest eggs of any amniote — vanished around 1000 AD, likely thanks to humans. What are they called?
Elephant bird are extinct flightless birds belonging to the order Aepyornithiformes that were native to the island of Madagascar.
Known regionally in Shropshire as the 'plum bird,' this small European finch, scientifically Pyrrhula pyrrhula, was the original bird to carry its common English name — which species?
Eurasian bullfinch (Pyrrhula pyrrhula) is a small passerine bird in the finch family, Fringillidae.
Madagascar's largest carnivore, this slender, long-tailed mammal evolved cougar-like features independently and climbs trees head-first thanks to flexible ankles — what is it?
Fossa (animal) (Cryptoprocta ferox; FOSS- or) is a slender, long-tailed, cat-like mammal that is endemic to Madagascar.
The largest of four living anteater species, this terrestrial mammal of Central and South America is known for its elongated snout, bushy tail, and long foreclaws. What is it?
Giant anteater (Myrmecophaga tridactyla) is an insectivorous mammal native to Central and South America.
This North Atlantic member of the true cod family is a fisheries staple in northern Europe, often smoked into varieties like Finnan haddie and the Arbroath smokie — what is it?
Haddock (Melanogrammus aeglefinus) is a saltwater ray-finned fish from the family Gadidae, the true cods.

This extinct human species from the Middle Pleistocene may represent the last common ancestor of modern humans, Neanderthals, and Denisovans — or a completely separate lineage altogether — what species is it?
Homo heidelbergensis is a species of archaic human from the Middle Pleistocene of Europe and Africa, as well as potentially Asia depending on the taxonomic convention used.

Dubbed the 'saviour of mothers,' this 19th-century Hungarian doctor demonstrated that a simple hygiene practice could drastically cut deaths from childbed fever, decades before germ theory was widely accepted — who is he?

Ignaz Semmelweis (1 July 1818 - 13 August 1865) was a Hungarian medical doctor and scientist of German descent who was an early pioneer of antiseptic procedures and was described as the "saviour of mothers".
The first woman ever to chair the Federal Reserve, she later became the first woman to serve as U.S. Treasury secretary — a Brooklyn-born, Yale-trained economist. Who is she?
Janet Yellen (born August 13, 1946) is an American economist who served as the 78th United States secretary of the treasury from 2021 to 2025 and as chair of the Federal Reserve from 2014 to 2018.

Sharing the 1973 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, this ethologist was among the first to decode the honey bee's waggle dance — a theory greeted with such skepticism that it took decades to be vindicated. Who was he?
Karl von Frisch (20 November 1886 - 12 June 1982) was a German-Austrian ethologist who received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1973, along with Nikolaas Tinbergen and Konrad Lorenz.

Which citrus-scented perennial herb in the mint family, whose genus name Melissa comes from the Greek for 'honey bee,' is naturalized worldwide after originating in the Mediterranean and Central Asia?
Lemon balm (Melissa officinalis) is a perennial herbaceous plant in the mint family.
Dubbed the 'Queen of QVC' for her long-running shopping show and holding over 120 patents, this American entrepreneur is also an investor on the reality series Shark Tank — who is she?
Lori Greiner is an American television personality and entrepreneur.

This Milanese thinker was the first woman to write a mathematics handbook and the first appointed a mathematics professor — though she spent her final decades on theology and serving the poor. Who was she?
Maria Gaetana Agnesi (16 May 1718 - 9 January 1799) was a Milanese mathematician, philosopher, theologian, and humanitarian.
Despite little formal education, this self-made English scientist established the concept of the electromagnetic field and uncovered the principles behind electromagnetic induction — who is he?
Michael Faraday (22 September 1791 - 25 August 1867) was an English chemist and physicist who contributed vastly to the study of electrochemistry and electromagnetism.

Though its 83 species can grow as tall as trees, this genus is technically herbaceous, its 'trunk' just tightly wrapped leaf stalks, and it gives us edible bananas, plantains, and fiber for cloth — what genus is it?
Musa (plant) is one of three genera in the family Musaceae.

First described in 1766 by naturalist Peter Simon Pallas, this sole living member of its genus sports a white throat patch and, in males only, a pair of short horns — what is this large Asian antelope called?
Nilgai (Boselaphus tragocamelus) (literally meaning "blue cow") is the largest antelope in Asia.
Triggered by repeated tension on the growth plate of the upper shinbone from running or jumping sports, this condition causes a tender bump below the kneecap in teens — what is it?
Osgood–Schlatter disease (OSD) is inflammation of the patellar ligament at the tibial tuberosity (apophysitis) usually affecting adolescents during growth spurts.
About 3,000 varieties of this apple-like fruit exist worldwide, and its fermented juice is known as perry — which fruit is it?
Pear are a genus of trees, Pyrus, in the family Rosaceae, that bear an edible apple-like fruit of the same name.
Native to Chile and Peru and cultivated since Inca times, this nightshade fruit is known in English as the Cape gooseberry or goldenberry — what is its scientific name?
Physalis peruviana is a species of plant in the nightshade family (Solanaceae) native to Chile and Peru.
Element number 19, this silvery alkali metal reacts so eagerly with air that it forms flaky white peroxide within seconds — and its symbol K comes from the Neo-Latin word kalium. What is it?
Potassium is a chemical element; it has symbol K (from Neo-Latin kalium) and atomic number 19.
Its blossoms are a beloved symbol of early spring throughout East Asia, and its crunchy fruit is marketed globally as the Asian or nashi pear - which tree species?
Pyrus pyrifolia is a species of pear tree native to southern China and northern Indochina that has been introduced to Korea, Japan and other parts of the world.

An emeritus fellow of an Oxford college and the first-ever holder of a professorship for the public understanding of science, this British evolutionary biologist is also known as a prominent atheist author — who is he?
Richard Dawkins (born 26 March 1941) is a British evolutionary biologist, zoologist, science communicator, noted atheist, and author.
This Indian-American executive succeeded Steve Ballmer as CEO of a major tech company in 2014 after running its cloud and enterprise division — who is he?
Satya Nadella (born 19 August 1967) is an Indian-American business executive.

Built for the Marine Corps by adding a third engine and a seventh main rotor blade to an earlier heavy-lift helicopter, this aircraft entered service in 1981 and flies from Navy ships — which helicopter?
Sikorsky CH-53E Super Stallion is a heavy lift helicopter operated by the United States military.
Doctors examine the color of this coughed-up airway mucus — greenish or yellow tints can hint at infection, though not which organism caused it — what is it?
Sputum is mucus that is coughed up from the lower airways (the trachea and bronchi).
This Turkish businesswoman served as one of her father's chief advisers back in 2013, when he held the office of prime minister and later became Turkey's president — who is she?
Sümeyye Erdoğan (ne Erdoan; born 22 August 1985) is a Turkish businesswoman and the daughter of President Recep Tayyip Erdoan.
This genus of coniferous evergreen in the cypress family includes five species — two native to North America, three to eastern Asia — and is sister to the genus Thujopsis. Name the genus?
Thuja is a genus of coniferous tree or shrub in the Cupressaceae (cypress family).

This flowering plant in the ginger family is native to the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia, requiring temperatures between 68 and 86°F and high rainfall. Its rhizomes are gathered and can be used fresh or dried for consumption and dyeing — what is it?
Turmeric is a flowering plant in the ginger family Zingiberaceae. Turmeric powder has a warm, bitter, black pepper-like flavor and earthy, mustard-like aroma.
This pungent Japanese condiment, ground from the rhizome of a plant related to horseradish and mustard, traditionally accompanies sushi. What is it?
A white, water-insoluble powder with the formula ZnO, this compound turns up in everything from sunscreens and calamine lotion to batteries and semiconductors — name this compound?
Zinc oxide is an inorganic compound with the formula ZnO. Although it occurs naturally as the mineral zincite, most zinc oxide is produced synthetically.
Made by the adrenal glands, this hormone powers the fight-or-flight response — boosting blood flow to muscles, dilating pupils and raising blood sugar by hitting alpha and beta receptors. What is it?
Adrenaline: Hormone and medication. It appears as a white microcrystalline granule.
Called lucerne in the UK, Australia and New Zealand, this perennial legume has been grown as livestock fodder since ancient times — which plant?
Alfalfa: Plant species in pea family.
A member of the aminopenicillin class, this oral antibiotic is a go-to for ear infections, strep throat, and pneumonia — and is often paired with clavulanic acid. What is it?
NATO code-named 'Condor,' this Soviet-designed four-engine giant is the largest military transport aircraft still flying today — which aircraft?

Antonov An-124 Ruslan: Soviet military transport aircraft. Assembly of the first aircraft begun in 1979; the An-124 (which was sometimes referred to as the An-40 in the West) performed its maiden flight on 24 December 1982.
Writing in 499 CE that he was 23 years old, this pioneering Indian scholar's explicit discussion of the relativity of motion marks him as an early physicist too — who was he?
Native to the steppes of Central Asia, this two-humped pack animal's cold and drought tolerance made it indispensable to Silk Road caravans — what is it?
Bactrian camel: Species of mammal of Asia.
This steroid medication treats everything from rheumatoid arthritis to psoriasis, and can even be given to speed a premature baby's lung development before birth — what is it?
Betamethasone: Steroid medication. It can be taken by mouth, injected into a muscle, or applied to the skin, typically in cream, lotion, or liquid forms.
Launched as the 7X7 program in 1978 and designed to complement the larger 747, which American wide-body airliner first entered service with United Airlines in 1982?
Too small to fuse hydrogen but massive enough to briefly burn deuterium, these objects between 13 and 80 Jupiter masses cool over time through spectral classes M, L, T, and Y — what are they called?
With more than 220 species and over 26,000 registered cultivars, this flowering plant genus includes the very species whose leaves are processed into tea worldwide — which genus?
Camellia: Genus of flowering plants in the tea family.
A woody shrub native to South America, this starchy tuber yields tapioca and, when grated and toasted, becomes Brazil's farofa and West Africa's garri — what crop is it?
Cassava: Staple crop. Although a perennial plant, cassava is extensively cultivated in tropical and subtropical regions as an annual crop for its edible starchy tuberous root.
Known by the common name 'greater celandine,' this perennial flowering plant belongs to the poppy family and is native to Europe and western Asia — what's its scientific name?
Chelidonium majus: Species of flowering plant in the poppy family. One of two species in the genus Chelidonium, it is native to Europe and western Asia and introduced widely in North America.
Dubbed the 'father of information theory,' this polymath was the first to apply Boolean algebra to digital circuits and helped found the field of artificial intelligence — who is he?

A summer migrant to Europe and Asia that winters in Africa, this bird tricks other species into raising its young by laying eggs that mimic the host's, and even disguises itself as a hawk — what bird is it?
Common cuckoo: Species of bird. It is a brood parasite, which means it lays eggs in the nests of other bird species, particularly of dunnocks, meadow pipits, and reed warblers.

This blood-feeding parasitic insect, scientifically Pthirus pubis, typically lives in coarse body hair and diverged from a gorilla-infecting relative about 3.3 million years ago — what is it commonly called?
Crab louse: Species of insect. The crab louse or pubic louse (Pthirus pubis) is an insect that is an obligate ectoparasite of humans, feeding exclusively on blood.
This Swedish tech entrepreneur founded and chairs a streaming giant, with a net worth estimated at $8.7 billion in December 2025 — who is he?
This bodily process breaks large food molecules into water-soluble components through both mechanical action like chewing and chemical action from enzymes — what's it called?
Digestion: Biological process of breaking down food.
Sometimes nicknamed 'math dyslexia' even though it's a distinct condition, this learning disorder involves persistent difficulty understanding numbers and performing calculations — what is it called?
This Italian-American physicist discovered two elements, technetium and astatine, plus the antiproton — the last earning him a share of the 1959 Nobel Prize in Physics. Who was he?
Emilio Segrè: Italian-American nuclear physicist and radiochemist (1905–1989)
Marketed under brand names like Arcoxia, this selective COX-2 inhibitor developed by Merck was approved in 63 countries by 2007 — everywhere, notably, except the United States — what is the drug?
In this common vision condition, distant objects appear sharp but close-up objects blur because light focuses behind the retina instead of on it - what is it?
Farsightedness: Eye condition in which light is focused behind instead of on the retina.
The lightest halogen, this pale yellow gas is so reactive that several 19th-century chemists died or were injured trying to isolate it, until Henri Moissan finally succeeded in 1886 — which element?
Fluorine: Chemical element with atomic number 9 (F)
Born in Pisa in 1564, this Italian polymath has been crowned the father of observational astronomy and the scientific method — and was among the earliest tinkerers to build a thermoscope. Who is he?
Galileo Galilei: Italian physicist and astronomer (1564–1642)
Despite centuries of use in Korean and Chinese traditional medicine, no clinical evidence supports health claims for this Panax-genus root, often sold as a dietary supplement — what is it?
Ginseng: Root of a plant used in herbal preparations.
This junctional area between the torso and thigh, where the lower abdominal wall meets the leg, is commonly strained in a familiar sports injury — what is it called?
Groin: Area between the torso and the thigh. In human anatomy, the groin, also known as the inguinal region or iliac region, is the junctional area between the torso and the thigh.
This wingless insect spends its entire life on the human scalp, sipping blood, and can neither fly nor jump — its short stumpy legs can't even walk well on a flat surface. What tiny freeloader is it?
Head louse: Insect parasite of humans.
This academic discipline studies the methods, sources, and interpretive approaches historians use when writing about the past — what's it called?
Historiography: Study of the methods used by historians.
A yellow-flowered perennial whose leaves look perforated by translucent glands, this plant is famed in folklore and traditional medicine under a saintly common name — what is its botanical name?
Hypericum perforatum: Flowering plant in the St John's wort family.
Endemic to semiarid central-eastern Australia and also called the "fierce snake," this elapid was rediscovered in 1972 after nearly 90 years of obscurity — what is it?
Inland taipan: Extremely venomous snake native to Australia.

This Dutch microscopist showed that an insect's egg, larva, pupa, and adult are all one animal, pioneered the microscope in dissections, and in 1658 became the first to observe red blood cells — who was he?
Jan Swammerdam: Dutch biologist and microscopist (1637–1680)
Equal to the work done when a one-newton force moves an object one metre, this SI unit of energy is named for a 19th-century English physicist — which unit?
Joule: SI unit of energy. The joule ( JOOL, or JOWL; symbol: J) is the unit of energy in the International System of Units (SI).
Living as a recluse in a log house outside Kaluga, this Russian pioneer of rocket science inspired both Wernher von Braun and the architects of the Soviet space program — who is he?
Also known as Peruvian ginseng, this Andean root crop is grown at high altitude in Peru and Bolivia and exported worldwide as a dietary powder — what plant is it?
Lepidium meyenii: Plant species native to South America.
This American WWII twin-engine, twin-boom fighter carried its pilot alone in a central nacelle and served as fighter-bomber, night fighter, and long-range escort — which aircraft was it?
Lockheed P-38 Lightning: American twin-engined fighter of WWII. The Lockheed P-38 Lightning is an American single-seat, twin-engined fighter aircraft that was used during World War II.
Occurring naturally as the mineral brucite, this poorly soluble white solid neutralizes stomach acid in a well-known antacid — which compound?
Magnesium hydroxide: Inorganic compound of formula Mg(OH)2.
Among the first women in Canada to earn a medical doctorate, this physician-chemist is best known for her 1913 work with Leonor Michaelis on enzyme kinetics — who was she?
Maud Menten: Canadian physician and chemist (1879–1960)
Marketed under brand names like Quaalude and Sopor, this sedative was pulled from commercial production in the mid-1980s due to widespread misuse — which drug?

A hemiparasitic plant that taps into its host tree via a structure called the haustorium to steal water and nutrients, its European species was introduced to Northern California in 1900 — what plant is it?
Mistletoe: Common name for various parasitic plants.
Considered a cultural universal present in every human society, this medium arranges sound into harmony, melody, and rhythm through composition, improvisation, and performance — what is it?
Music: Form of art using sound.
Erected by entomologist Francis Walker back in 1855, this genus of moths belongs to the family Lasiocampidae — which genus?
This burrowing, semiaquatic South American rodent munches river-plant stems and was shipped worldwide by fur farmers, only to become a destructive invasive pest — which animal is it?
Nutria: Semi-aquatic rodent from South America.
Farmed largely around a South African town, this flightless bird is the heaviest bird alive and can sprint 70 km/h — the fastest of any bird on land. What is it?
Ostrich: Genus of largest living birds.
This American physician-turned-clown founded the Gesundheit Institute in 1989 and travels the world dressing up to bring humor to hospital patients — who is he?
What is this — “Abnormal growth of scar tissue within the penis”?

Peyronie's disease: Abnormal growth of scar tissue within the penis. The plaques cause abnormal curvature, pain, penile deformities (e.g., narrowing or indentation), and usually erectile dysfunction, particularly during erection.
This self-limiting skin condition begins with a single “herald patch” before smaller scaly spots erupt days later, usually clearing up on its own within three months — which condition?
Pityriasis rosea: Skin disease. It usually lasts less than three months and goes away without treatment.
Used to disinfect skin before and after surgery, this antiseptic can cause kidney problems and high blood sodium if applied to large wounds, and comes as a liquid, ointment, or powder — what is it?
Povidone-iodine: Antiseptic solution. Povidone-iodine (PVP-I), also known as iodopovidone, is an antiseptic used for skin disinfection before and after surgery.

Covering the asymmetric relationship between citizens and the state — including constitutional, administrative, tax, and criminal matters — this branch of the legal system contrasts with the branch governing relationships between individuals — which branch?
Public law: Law governing government actions.
One of the oldest groups of eukaryotic seaweed, this phylum boasts over 7,000 species — mostly marine, though about 5% live in freshwater habitats. What group is it?
Red algae: Division of plant life.

Also called black locust or false acacia, this deciduous legume-family tree is native to just a few small pockets of the United States but has been planted so widely it's now considered invasive elsewhere — which tree?
Robinia pseudoacacia: Species of tree native to North America.
Containing the potent compound salvinorin A, this plant used by Mazatec shamans for spiritual healing sparked a US media panic around 2007 after being shared in online videos — which plant?
Salvia divinorum: Species of plant. The leaves contain the potent compound salvinorin A and can induce a dissociative state and hallucinations.
Ejaculated through the urethra and containing fructose plus enzymes that help sperm survive their journey to fertilize an egg, this bodily fluid is also collected for animal breeding. What is it?
Semen: Reproductive biofluid of male or hermaphroditic animals.
This altered state cycles between REM and non-REM modes, and despite outward stillness it still produces active brain patterns — more reactive than a coma. What is it?
Sleep: Naturally recurring resting state of mind and body.
Lacking any nervous, digestive, or circulatory system, these ancient sea-bound filter feeders pump water through pore-riddled bodies using flagella to survive — what are they?
Sponge: Animals of the phylum Porifera.
Nicknamed the "Super Flanker" and derived from the Su-27, this twin-engine, supermaneuverable Russian air superiority fighter first flew as a prototype in 1988 — what is it?
Sukhoi Su-35: Upgraded series of the Su-27 fighter aircraft.
Nicknamed the brown raptor, this nocturnal bird of prey nests in tree hollows across Europe and is so territorial that evicted youngsters may starve — what is it?
Tawny owl: Stocky medium-sized owl species.

Marked by platelet counts that fall too low — sometimes below 50,000 per microliter and requiring emergency care — this blood disorder is the most common coagulation problem in ICU patients — what is it called?
Thrombocytopenia: Abnormally low levels of platelets in the blood.
